content: Brood parasites are organisms that exploit the parental care of other individuals, either of the same species (intraspecific brood parasitism) or of different species (interspecific brood parasitism), to raise their offspring. This strategy allows the parasitic parent to avoid the energetic costs of rearing their young or building nests, enabling them to allocate more resources to foraging, producing additional offspring, or other activities. In many monogamous bird species, males may engage in extra-pair matings, resulting in offspring sired outside the primary pair bond. This behavior allows males to avoid the parental investment associated with raising their offspring. Females, however, take this strategy further by laying their eggs in the nests of other individuals. Intraspecific brood parasitism is observed in several duck species, such as the Goldeneye (Bucephala clangula), where females deposit their eggs in the nests of conspecifics. Interspecific brood parasitism, on the other hand, is exemplified by species such as Old World cuckoos in Eurasia and Australia, cowbirds and Black-headed Ducks in the Americas, and indigobirds, whydahs, and honeyguides in Africa. Most avian brood parasites are highly specialized, targeting a single host species or a small group of closely related species. However, some, like the Brown-headed Cowbird, are generalists and parasitize a wide range of host species—221 known hosts in the case of the Brown-headed Cowbird. Typically, brood parasites lay only one egg per host nest, although exceptions exist, such as multiple cowbird females using the same host nest. The Common Cuckoo is particularly notable for its specialization: while the species as a whole parasitizes a variety of hosts, individual females specialize in a single host species. This specialization is facilitated by genetic inheritance of egg coloration, which is passed exclusively through the maternal line, enabling females to lay eggs that mimic those of their chosen host. Female cuckoos are thought to imprint on the host species that raised them and subsequently parasitize only that species. Male cuckoos, however, mate across different maternal lines, ensuring genetic diversity within the population. The mechanisms by which female cuckoos select their hosts remain unclear, but several hypotheses have been proposed. These include genetic inheritance of host preference, imprinting on the host species during development, returning to the site of their own birth and choosing a host randomly (natal philopatry), selecting hosts based on preferred nest sites (nest-site hypothesis), and choosing hosts based on preferred habitat (habitat-selection hypothesis). Experimental evidence has provided the strongest support for the nest-site and habitat-selection hypotheses. Specialist avian brood parasites have evolved a range of adaptations to enhance their reproductive success. Mimetic eggs, which closely resemble the eggs of the host species, are a nearly universal adaptation among these parasites. Even generalist species like the Brown-headed Cowbird may have evolved egg coloration that mimics those of multiple host species. Most brood parasites remove one of the host's eggs when laying their own, either during the same visit or in a separate visit before or after parasitism. This behavior may serve to prevent the host from detecting the parasitism or to reduce competition for resources once the parasitic chick hatches. Brood parasites also tend to have shorter egg incubation periods and faster nestling growth rates, giving their offspring a competitive advantage over the host's young. In some cases, parasitic nestlings eliminate their nestmates by ejecting them from the nest or killing them with specialized hooks on their mandibles, which fall off after a few days. The Mafia hypothesis has been proposed to explain why many host species continue to care for the offspring of brood parasites, despite the significant costs to their own reproductive success. According to this hypothesis, brood parasites manipulate their hosts through aggressive behaviors. If a host detects and rejects a parasitic egg, the parasite may retaliate by destroying the host's nest, killing its nestlings, or otherwise reducing its reproductive success. Two avian species, the Brown-headed Cowbird (Molothrus ater) in North America and the Great Spotted Cuckoo (Clamator glandarius) in Europe, are thought to exhibit this mafia-like behavior. For example, experiments conducted by Soler et al. in Spain demonstrated that European Magpie (Pica pica) nests from which Great Spotted Cuckoo eggs were removed experienced significantly higher rates of predation compared to nests that accepted the parasitic eggs. Similarly, experiments by Hoover et al. in North America showed that Prothonotary Warbler (Protonotaria citrea) nests that rejected Brown-headed Cowbird eggs were depredated at much higher rates than those that accepted the eggs. Host species have evolved various counteradaptations to mitigate the impact of brood parasitism. The most effective strategy is to prevent parasitism altogether, which can be achieved by selecting nest sites that are difficult for parasites to access, initiating incubation early to remain on the nest during the parasite's visit, and aggressively defending their territory. Birds that nest in colonies may also benefit from group defense against parasites. Once parasitism has occurred, hosts may attempt to eject the parasitic egg, either by grasping it with their beak (grasp ejection) or puncturing it (puncture ejection). However, this behavior carries risks, such as mistakenly ejecting their own eggs or damaging their eggs in the process. Some hosts that do not eject parasitic eggs may abandon the parasitized nest and start anew, although this strategy becomes less effective in areas with high parasitism rates, as the new nest is likely to be parasitized again. Brood parasitism is not limited to birds. Among insects, cuckoo bees are brood parasites that lay their eggs in the nest cells of other bees. These insects are often referred to as kleptoparasites rather than brood parasites. Similarly, cuckoo wasps lay their eggs in the nests of other wasps, such as Potter Wasps and Mud Dauber Wasps. Many other wasp lineages have independently evolved similar parasitic behaviors.
